beginner.question: A finite difference approximates a derivative using nearby function values instead of computing it exactly.
options: True
False
beginner.explanation: True. That is the definition of a finite-difference approximation: estimate f’(x) from two (or more) evaluations of f near x, rather than differentiating a closed-form expression.
optionExplanations: Correct — that’s exactly what a finite difference is.
Incorrect — this is the core definition of a finite difference.

beginner.question: Which formula is the forward-difference approximation to f’(x)?
options: (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h
(f(x) - f(x-h)) / h
f(x+h) - f(x-h)
beginner.explanation: The forward difference uses the current point and one step ahead: (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h.
optionExplanations: Correct — current point plus one step ahead, divided by h.
This is the backward difference, not forward.
This is the centered difference, not forward.
Missing the division by 2h; also this is the centered numerator alone.

beginner.question: Which formula is the backward-difference approximation to f’(x)?
options: (f(x) - f(x-h)) / h
(f(x+h) - f(x)) / h
beginner.explanation: The backward difference uses the current point and one step behind: (f(x) - f(x-h)) / h.
optionExplanations: Correct.
This is the forward difference.
This is the centered difference.
This averages the two points; it does not approximate a derivative.

beginner.question: Which formula is the centered-difference approximation to f’(x)?
options: (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h
(f(x) - f(x-h)) / h
(f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / h
beginner.explanation: The centered difference uses one step ahead and one step behind, divided by 2h: (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / (2h).
optionExplanations: Correct.
This is the forward difference.
This is the backward difference.
Missing the factor of 2 in the denominator.

beginner.question: The backward difference is the natural choice at the end of a data series, where there is no point "ahead" to use.
options: True
False
beginner.explanation: True. With no data beyond the last point, only the current and previous points are available, which is exactly what backward difference uses.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this is precisely why backward difference is used at a series’ end.

beginner.question: The centered difference is generally more accurate than the forward or backward difference for the same step size h.
options: True
False
beginner.explanation: True. Centered difference has O(h²) error, while forward/backward have O(h) error — for the same h, centered is more accurate.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — centered difference’s error shrinks faster as h shrinks.

beginner.question: What does the MATLAB function gradient(y) compute, when y is a vector of function values sampled at equally spaced points?
options: An approximate derivative at each sample point, using centered differences in the interior and one-sided differences at the ends
The exact symbolic derivative of the data
The integral of y using the trapezoidal rule
The maximum slope anywhere in the data
beginner.explanation: gradient(y) automatically applies centered differences everywhere it can and one-sided (forward/backward) differences at the two endpoints, where a centered estimate isn’t possible.
optionExplanations: Correct.
gradient() is numerical, not symbolic — there is no exact closed form involved.
That describes trapz(), not gradient().
gradient() returns an estimate at every point, not just the maximum.

beginner.question: Which MATLAB function estimates the spacing between consecutive x-values, useful when you’re not sure the samples are perfectly uniform?

gradient(x)
sum(x)
sort(x)

gradient() estimates a derivative, not spacing.
sum() adds all elements together — unrelated to spacing.
sort() reorders elements — unrelated to spacing.

beginner.question: Why can’t MATLAB always compute a derivative symbolically for a function used in this course?
options: The "function" is often raw experimental data, or a simulation with no continuous closed form to differentiate in the first place
MATLAB has no way to compute any derivatives at all
Symbolic differentiation is always less accurate than a finite difference
MATLAB only supports derivatives of polynomials
beginner.explanation: Sensor readings, biomarker samples, and step-by-step simulations don’t have a formula to begin with, so there’s nothing to symbolically differentiate — a finite-difference estimate from nearby values is the only option.
optionExplanations: Correct.
MATLAB can do symbolic differentiation on functions that do have a closed form; the issue is when there isn’t one.
Symbolic differentiation is exact when it applies; the issue is applicability, not accuracy.
MATLAB’s symbolic engine is not restricted to polynomials.

beginner.question: Truncation error in a finite-difference approximation shrinks as the step size h shrinks.
options: True
False
beginner.explanation: True. Truncation error comes from the Taylor-series terms that were dropped; as h shrinks, those dropped terms (which scale with a positive power of h) shrink too.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — truncation error specifically shrinks with h; it’s round-off error that grows as h shrinks.

beginner.question: Round-off error in a finite-difference approximation grows as the step size h shrinks toward zero.
options: True
False
beginner.explanation: True. As h gets very small, f(x+h) and f(x) become nearly identical floating-point numbers, and subtracting them loses precision — this round-off error grows as h shrinks.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — round-off error grows, not shrinks, as h shrinks; it is truncation error that shrinks.

beginner.question: What is the practical consequence of truncation error shrinking while round-off error grows as h shrinks?
options: Total error has a minimum at some intermediate h, not at the smallest h possible
Total error always decreases as h shrinks, with no limit
Total error is unaffected by h
Total error only depends on round-off error, never on truncation error
beginner.explanation: The two error sources move in opposite directions as h changes, so their sum (total error) has a minimum somewhere in the middle — making h smaller and smaller eventually makes things worse, not better.
optionExplanations: Correct.
This ignores round-off error, which eventually dominates and increases total error.
Total error very much depends on h — that’s the entire point of the tradeoff.
Both sources contribute; truncation error dominates for larger h.

beginner.question: Differentiating raw, noisy experimental data directly (without smoothing first) tends to:
options: Amplify the noise, since each derivative estimate divides a small difference by a small h
Automatically remove the noise
Have no effect on the noise level
Only work if the data has been rounded to fewer decimal places
beginner.explanation: Dividing a noisy difference by a small h amplifies whatever noise was in the original signal — differentiation is a noise-amplifying operation, which is why smoothing (e.g. a moving average) usually comes first.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Differentiation does not remove noise — it tends to make it more visible.
The effect is not neutral; noise gets amplified.
Rounding is not a standard smoothing technique here and does not reliably help.

beginner.question: Big-O notation, like O(h) or O(h²), describes:

The exact numerical value of the error
The number of function evaluations used
The units of the derivative being estimated

beginner.question: For a scheme with O(h) error, halving h roughly halves the error.

False

beginner.question: For a scheme with O(h²) error, halving h roughly quarters the error.
options: True
False

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this is exactly what O(h²) scaling means.

A single unknown number, just like a static model
A plot, with no underlying equation

A one-time height measurement is static.

advanced.question: Deriving the forward difference from the Taylor series, f(x+h) = f(x) + f’(x)h + f’’(x)h²/2! + ..., which term is the leading (dominant) source of the forward difference’s truncation error?
options: f’’(x)h²/2!, divided by h, giving an O(h) term
f’(x)h, divided by h, giving an O(1) term
f(x), which does not depend on h at all
There is no truncation error in the forward difference
advanced.explanation: Rearranging for f’(x) and dividing the leftover terms by h, the first neglected term is f’’(x)h²/2! / h = f’’(x)h/2, which is O(h) — the leading error term.
optionExplanations: Correct.
The f’(x)h term is exactly what forward difference solves for; it is not error.
f(x) cancels out of the derivation entirely.
The forward difference definitely carries O(h) truncation error — that’s the whole point of the derivation.

advanced.question: Why does subtracting the backward Taylor expansion from the forward one (to derive the centered difference) cancel the f’’(x) term specifically?
options: f’’(x)h²/2! appears with the same sign in both expansions (even power of h), so subtracting cancels it, while the odd-power terms double instead
f’’(x) is always exactly zero for any function
The forward and backward expansions do not actually contain an f’’(x) term
Subtraction cancels every term except the very first one
advanced.explanation: f(x-h) has (-h)² = h² for the second-order term — same sign as in f(x+h) — so subtracting f(x-h) from f(x+h) cancels the even-order (f’’, f⁴, ...) terms and doubles the odd-order (f’, f’’’, ...) terms.
optionExplanations: Correct.
f’’(x) is generally nonzero; the cancellation is structural, not because the value is zero.
Both expansions do contain this term, which is exactly why the cancellation is meaningful.
Odd-order terms survive (doubled); it is specifically the even-order terms that cancel.
advanced.concept: Why centered difference cancels O(h²) error

advanced.question: A student computes f’(x) with h = 1e-3 and gets error 2.1e-4. They then try h = 1e-8, expecting a much smaller error, but the error is instead about 1e-8, worse than a naive O(h) prediction would suggest at that scale, and inconsistent as h shrinks further. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Round-off error from subtracting two nearly identical floating-point numbers has started to dominate the total error
The function being differentiated must not have a well-defined derivative
MATLAB has a hard-coded minimum step size of 1e-3
The forward-difference formula is simply wrong and should not be trusted at any h
advanced.explanation: At h = 1e-8, f(x+h) and f(x) are so close that their floating-point difference loses most of its significant digits — round-off error dominates at this scale, exactly the tradeoff the chapter describes.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Nothing in this scenario suggests the function itself is problematic — this is a floating-point precision effect.
MATLAB does not impose such a minimum; the effect described is a real numerical phenomenon at very small h.
The formula is correct; its truncation-error behavior is simply overtaken by round-off at extreme h.

advanced.question: For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 0, using the centered difference with h = 0.1, what is the estimate of f’(0)? (True value is cos(0) = 1.) Give your answer to 6 decimal places.
advanced.explanation: (sin(0.1) - sin(-0.1)) / 0.2 = (0.099833 - -0.099833) / 0.2 = 0.998334, very close to the true value 1, reflecting O(h²) accuracy.

advanced.question: For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 0, using the forward difference with h = 0.1, what is the estimate of f’(0)? Give your answer to 6 decimal places.
advanced.explanation: (sin(0.1) - sin(0)) / 0.1 = 0.099833 / 0.1 = 0.998334, noticeably farther from the true value 1 than the centered estimate at the same h — the O(h) vs O(h²) gap in action.

advanced.question: Which of the following would reduce the truncation error of a centered-difference estimate, all else being equal? Select all that apply.
options: Shrinking h, as long as round-off error hasn’t taken over yet
Switching from centered to forward difference at the same h
Using a higher-order finite-difference formula (more surrounding points) at the same h
Increasing h without bound
advanced.explanation: Shrinking h reduces O(h²) truncation error (until round-off dominates), and higher-order formulas that use more surrounding points can achieve even faster error decay (e.g. O(h⁴)) at the same h. Switching to forward difference would make truncation error worse, not better (O(h) vs O(h²)), and increasing h without bound increases truncation error.
commonMistakes: Assuming any change to the formula or step size improves accuracy, without checking whether it increases or decreases the truncation-error order.

advanced.question: You need the derivative of a signal at its very first sample, and only forward-in-time data exists at that point (no data before it). Which scheme must you use there, regardless of what you use elsewhere in the signal?

Centered difference, since it is always most accurate

Backward difference also requires a point behind x — impossible here.
A one-sided estimate is still possible and standard practice, even if less accurate than centered.

advanced.question: Put these steps in order for deriving the forward-difference formula (with its error term) from the Taylor series.

Recognize the result as the forward-difference formula plus an explicit error term
advanced.explanation: You start from the Taylor expansion, algebraically isolate f′(a), identify what got left behind (the O(h) term), and recognize the resulting expression as the forward difference with its error explicitly attached.

diff() only reports spacing — it does not alter or resample the data.
gradient(y, x) explicitly uses x to account for (possibly non-uniform) spacing between points.

advanced.question: For f(x) = x^3 at x = 0.5 with h = 0.15, which is closer to the analytically true derivative: the forward-difference estimate (0.9975) or the centered-difference estimate (0.7725)?
options: The centered-difference estimate, because its error is O(h²) rather than O(h)
The forward-difference estimate, because it uses a "later" point
They are always exactly equal
Neither — both are always equally inaccurate
advanced.explanation: Centered difference has O(h²) truncation error versus forward difference’s O(h) — for the same h, centered is expected to be closer to the true derivative, which computing both against 3x^2 at x=0.5 confirms here.

advanced.question: For f(x) = x^2 at x = 0.8 with h = 0.05, which is closer to the analytically true derivative: the forward-difference estimate (1.65) or the centered-difference estimate (1.6)?
options: The centered-difference estimate, because its error is O(h²) rather than O(h)
The forward-difference estimate, because it uses a "later" point

Referencing an updated value would make the loop run in the wrong order entirely
It only matters for systems with more than two state variables

expert.question: A model has one "fast" state variable (changes on a millisecond timescale) coupled to one "slow" state variable (changes over minutes). Forward Euler needs an extremely small h to remain stable, dictated entirely by the fast variable, even though the slow variable barely changes between steps. What term describes this situation, and what is the standard remedy?
options: Stiffness; use Backward Euler or a stiff solver (e.g. ode15s) so step size is dictated by accuracy needs, not stability limits
Resonance; use a larger step size to average out the fast oscillation
Divergence; the model is unsolvable as stated
Aliasing; resample the slow variable at a coarser rate
expert.explanation: This is the textbook definition of stiffness — a large gap between timescales that forces an explicit method into tiny steps for stability alone. Implicit or stiff-specific solvers decouple step size from that stability constraint.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Resonance is an unrelated physical phenomenon; using a larger step size on a stiff explicit simulation would make it unstable, not accurate.
The system is fully solvable; the issue is specific to explicit-method step-size requirements, not solvability.
Aliasing is a signal-processing sampling issue, not what is described here.
references: Unit 4 Review: Initial Value Problems & Euler’s Method

expert.question: You are asked to simulate a 4-compartment pharmacokinetic model (4 coupled ODEs) with Forward Euler. Design the state representation that keeps the update loop clean.
options: Store all 4 state variables as a single vector y at each time index, and update the whole vector each step: y(:,k+1) = y(:,k) + f(t(k), y(:,k))*h
Use 4 entirely separate, unrelated scripts, one per compartment, run independently
Store the 4 variables as 4 separate scalars, re-declared fresh inside every loop iteration
Avoid Euler’s method entirely for any system with more than 2 state variables
expert.explanation: Generalizing the two-state-variable pattern, stacking all state variables into one vector and stepping the whole vector each iteration scales cleanly to any number of coupled equations, keeping the loop structure identical regardless of how many compartments there are.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Separate independent scripts would break the coupling between compartments, which is the entire point of a coupled model.
Re-declaring fresh scalars each iteration would discard the previous step’s state, breaking the simulation.
Euler’s method generalizes to any number of coupled first-order equations via vector state — no such limit exists.

references: Unit 4 Review: Initial Value Problems & Euler’s Method

expert.question: You compare a Forward Euler simulation (h=0.001, thousands of cheap steps) against a Backward Euler simulation (h=0.5, few but fzero-based steps) of the same stiff system, and both finish successfully. The Forward Euler run takes far longer in wall-clock time. What does this demonstrate about "stability" versus "cost"?
options: Stability determines the SMALLEST usable step size for an explicit method on a stiff problem, which can make even a "successful" explicit run computationally expensive compared to an implicit alternative
Stability and cost are unrelated; the timing difference must be a coincidence
Forward Euler must have a bug, since Backward Euler is always faster
The wall-clock difference proves Backward Euler is more accurate
expert.explanation: Even when both methods are stable and "work," an explicit method’s stability constraint can force a step size so small that the sheer number of steps dominates runtime — exactly the situation stiffness describes, and exactly why implicit methods exist despite their higher per-step cost.
optionExplanations: Correct.
The relationship is direct and well-understood, not coincidental — this is the practical consequence of stiffness.
Nothing here implies a bug; both methods can be correctly implemented and still differ enormously in cost.
Wall-clock time reflects cost, not accuracy — Backward Euler is more stable/efficient here, not necessarily more accurate at a comparable cost.
references: Unit 4 Review: Initial Value Problems & Euler’s Method

expert.question: A decay model dy/dt = -0.45y is simulated with Forward Euler at h=0.4 and separately at h=0.1, both remaining stable. Which run is expected to more closely match the exact analytical solution, and why?

The h=0.4 run, because larger steps average out more error
Both are identical, since the equation is linear
Neither — Forward Euler cannot be applied to decay equations
expert.explanation: Forward Euler’s global error is O(h); a smaller step size (h=0.1) is expected to produce a more accurate result than a larger one (h=0.4), all else equal.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Larger steps increase error under O(h) scaling; they do not average it away.
Linearity of the ODE does not make different step sizes produce identical numerical results.
Forward Euler applies to decay equations just as readily as growth equations.
